results.title: Only contact with fixed points binds loops, and it binds them into atoms
results.statement: With one selector per loop of permutation contact, the shape of the loop constraints is the nerve of the holonomies' fixed-point sets, every tie or knot among loops is an atom, free contact binds nothing, and a knot among k loops needs k+1 witness values (Lean). Every simplicial complex arises as such a shape.

results.title: The holes of permutation networks are shallow
results.statement: Two-witness linear reasoning over a ring R misses an impossible permutation network exactly when R can write 1 from the holonomy-orbit sizes, and over the integers first on five values with orbits 2 and 3. Pinning one witness, or holding three witnesses at once, refutes every impossible network over every ring.

results.title: Competing pairwise rules make only the not-all-equal triangle knot
results.statement: Read by competition, so that a system allows the states breaking the fewest rules, rules on pairs make exactly the four not-all-equal knots on three variables, the frustrated triangles, and no knot on four or more; with hidden variables they make every knot. Read strictly, they make none.

results.title: Knots are patterns constrained as a whole and free in every part
results.statement: Read on allowed states with erasure as forgetting, a knot is a relation constrained as a whole and free in every part: two loops and a contact have exactly 34, from the single clause ¬A ∨ ¬B ∨ c to parity, which hides one full bit. No 2-CNF with witnesses defines a knot, while three-literal clauses with named intermediates define every knot.

results.title: Only group-like knots remember a loop
results.statement: A ring of knots joined through witnesses excludes a middle pattern exactly when every transfer along it is a permutation and an odd number swap, so it composes into a knot or nothing (Lean). Only parity has all-permutation transfers and keeps one full bit at every length; other knots' memory fades with the loop's length.

results.title: Native star knots end exactly at the freezing threshold of random colourings
results.statement: On the d-regular tree with the broadcast colouring, the star knot 'not all q colours used' exists at every degree but is native only below the freezing threshold, d = 6, 10, 15 for q = 3, 4, 5 (certified exactly), where its nativity drops discontinuously from 1 to below 0.0011. Planted random regular graphs match the tree at every measured radius, so native knots in random colourings end exactly where typical solutions freeze.

results.title: Emergence under the source-aware reading depends on the law (entropy) and on the world (frozen or flexible)
results.statement: Under the source-aware reading emergence depends on the law and the world: a linear law has native knots at every world or at none (on Z^d exactly when it has positive entropy; Ledrappier's law and Tseitin plus gauge are frozen), while proper 3-colourings have frozen worlds where the star knot 'not all distinct' is not native and dense flexible worlds where it is. Native loops are not sufficient: the hard-core law is flexible everywhere but has no knot.

results.title: Colouring knots exist exactly on Gallai trees and compose by fusion
results.statement: In the q-colouring law, hidden witnesses with q neighbours each give their visible leaves a K1-K3 knot exactly when the witness graph is a Gallai tree; otherwise they impose nothing. Gluing at a witness fuses two knots into one with multiplicative excluded mass, and a shared visible vertex is a hub, so knots here compose by fusion along Gallai trees, never into networks of distinct knots.

results.title: Ends supply open distinctions that the knot test cannot tell from loops, and the law decides which a system has
results.statement: In infinite parity systems an open distinction comes from a finite loop or from the ends; the 3-regular tree has a K1-K3 knot at every vertex without any loop, and no finite part or knot verdict tells the sources apart. The law decides the source: on the square grid Tseitin's vertex law has only loop-supplied openness, while Ledrappier's triangle law has no finite loop and every triangle is a knot opened by infinity.

results.title: At the base, three gives knots, but extension needs two-signed knots and memory needs reversible ones
results.statement: Every law on bits is pairwise, frozen (only 'not all on' or 'not all off' knots, which never compose) or transmitting, where knots compose exactly when they force a shared distinction oppositely and chains grow. Lasting memory of loops holds exactly when all polymorphisms are affine, exactly when bounded local reasoning fails, and hardness lies only inside transmission with memory.

results.title: A knot hides at most one bit from its pairs, and a network at most one bit per cycle, filled only by parity
results.statement: The bits a relation on bits hides from its pairs vanish exactly at two-literal clauses, reach one bit only for parity among knots, reach about n - log2 log2 n on n bits through covering arrays, and the statistical version vanishes only on least sets of pairwise energies, so not-all-equal is the only silent knot. With hidden joints, a network of knots hides at most one bit per independent cycle, exactly for parity, and frustrating patches add up.

results.title: In affine chains, persistence and composition across time are decided by two row sequences of M^T
results.statement: For three-ring chains with linear or affine rules and affine contact laws, a contact's value at lag T is the parity of the first-row cells in its row of M^T plus a constant, so it binds two rings exactly when that row meets both, and the chain composes when the far contact's row meets both end rings. The rows are eventually periodic, so iterating them until they repeat decides every lag exactly.

results.title: One band makes the torus from a loop of rings
results.statement: One band inserted into a loop of n equally spaced rule-60 rings, each new ring joined to its partner on both sides, gives the n x 2 torus, and every n x m torus with n at least 3 and m at least 2 has a half-turn at every contact. So a uniform local law makes the torus from a loop at its first step and keeps every contact persistent at every stage.

results.title: Distance across time is native: the cut length is the ring graph's distance, the time length the contact graph's directed distance
results.statement: In networks of rule-60 rings, a route isolated by freezing makes its far contact first need the near ring at lag g L + 1, additively, so counted length is native (A40); the earliest need any freeze allows is g delta + 1, delta the directed contact-graph distance, and the most disjoint cuts separating two rings is their ring-graph distance. Without freezing, the first need is that light cone filtered by the parity of shortest routes, not a metric.

results.title: A network of rings reads its genus: two rings of cuts per handle keep one piece
results.statement: In any network of rule-60 rings, the pieces read from which uncut contacts need which rings after a cut are exactly the components of the ring graph without the cut contacts. So a family of rings of cuts keeps the network in one piece exactly when it is independent in the surface's homology mod 2, which allows at most two per handle, as on the torus and on a persistent genus-2 network of 16 rings.

results.title: Lattices of rings grow by bands, not by single rings
results.statement: Every n x m torus of equally spaced rule-60 rings with n, m at least 3 has a half-turn at every contact, so growth by whole bands round the torus or by splitting every ring into blocks keeps every contact persistent at every stage. A single new ring breaks it with one contact, with two not side by side, or as a bubble on a corner from p to q whenever some contact is reached from q and reaches p.
results.issue: Qualification pending: "not by single rings" holds for rings attached to a network; a ring inserted with the contacts across the gap rejoined through it keeps every contact persistent on the twist torus (see GROW-PLAIN-20261109-001).

results.title: Intermittent composition across time is a strobed chain's composition, and in linear chains it is arrival
results.statement: In a chain of three rings the lags at which the far contact binds the end rings recur with the period P of the chain's T-step maps, so a chain observed at one residue modulo P composes at every observed lag or at none: intermittent composition is a strobed chain's composition, whose phase the chain does not fix. For linear or affine rules with affine contact laws the composing lags are exactly the arrival lags of both ends' influence.

results.title: Odd tori of rings compose everywhere, even tori never reach the antipode; rings of cuts separate when they bound
results.statement: On the square torus of equally spaced rings a contact needs a ring exactly when an odd number of contact-graph walks lead from it, counted by powers of x + 1/x + y + 1/y over GF(2), and every contact needs every ring on odd tori while none ever needs its antipodal ring on even tori. Cutting the contacts round any set of rings separates it, one ring of cuts round the torus does not, and two do.

results.title: Balanced loops of any number of rings persist at every size
results.statement: In a loop of r rule-60 rings the feedback is z(A + cA^-1), A a weighted cyclic shift, and when the contacts' positions sum to rs/2 every return to a contact cancels, so every contact binds both its rings at every lag at every ring size. The feedback is a finite sum exactly when r is a power of two.

results.title: Symmetric networks of loops persist at every size; where a loop meets a shared ring they cannot
results.statement: In networks of rule-60 rings a contact keeps its witnesses at every lag exactly when its returns cancel; a symmetry exchanging a contact's two rings cancels them, so loops, two rings sharing contacts, the Platonic networks and square, triangular and honeycomb lattices on a torus persist at every size. Where a two-contact ring meets a larger ring, one return of length 2 is unpaired and the witnesses lapse, as in every figure-eight and chord across a loop.

results.title: Balanced loops of rings persist at every size
results.statement: In loops of four rule-60 rings whose contacts read chain ends, the feedback returning round the loop cancels exactly when the contacts' positions sum to 2s, so each contact has a closed form over GF(2). Under a no-overlap condition every contact then binds both its rings at every lag at every ring size.

results.title: A path of contacts across time has a light cone, and on affine substrates every verdict is two row sequences per contact
results.statement: In a path of rings joined by shared contacts, the last contact cannot depend on the first ring before the lag one past the summed distances between the contacts of each middle ring, so the ends are bound only from then. For linear or affine rules and affine laws, a contact binds two rings at lag T exactly when its row of M^T meets both, so iterating rows until they repeat decides every verdict.

results.title: Only the sphere reads distance plainly: the plain first need fails on every flat torus but 26 and beyond a horizon on curved tilings
results.statement: Without freezing, every loop of rings, pair of rings and Platonic network reads distance at every size, while flat and hyperbolic tilings hide it beyond a horizon set by ring and face sizes, so exactly 26 tori read it. The smallest regular map that fails, a 13-ring twisted square torus, reads it in its mirror image, so no criterion by type, genus, curvature or size decides finite maps.
results.issue: Qualification pending: the 26 tori and "only the sphere at every size" hold for regular maps (rotation-invariant tori); thin tori of other shapes, such as every square torus holding (2, 0), read distance plainly at every size (see GROWN-DISTANCE-20261109-001).

results.title: Listening contacts never compose, and a shared chain carries the far ring only after crossing the middle ring
results.statement: In a chain of three rings, listening contacts, which read their rings and feed nothing back, never let the far contact depend on the far ring, so composition needs a contact the middle ring reads. With shared contacts the far contact cannot depend on the first ring before lag d + 1, d the contacts' distance on the middle ring, and with linear or affine rules a contact binds two rings exactly when its row of M^T meets both.

results.title: A contact binds two processes exactly when it is a parity of two remembering contact cells
results.statement: A contact cell reading one cell of each of two rings binds both at lag T exactly when neither ring's first row with the contact's first value decides its value, equivalently when forgetting either ring leaves it free, and a memoryless contact binds exactly when it is XOR or XNOR of two contact cells still depending on their first rows. Between linear rings the parity contact binds at every lag exactly when neither ring polynomial is nilpotent.

results.title: Two-apart one-sided additive paths compose at recurring lags at every ring size
results.statement: In four-ring paths with rule 60 or 102 on each ring and the middle contacts two apart, every contact binds both its rings at every lag at every ring size, and the last contact binds the end rings exactly where C(T - 3, m) is odd, m = 2, s - 2 or 2s - 6. By Lucas' theorem these lags recur, so all 64 families compose at recurring lags at every size, and at every lag none do.

results.title: One-sided additive paths of every length compose at recurring lags
results.statement: With n >= 3 rings of s >= 4 cells, rule 60 or 102 on each ring and every middle ring's contacts two apart, every contact persists and the last contact binds the first ring exactly when C(T - (n - 1), e) is odd, e the sum of k_j - 1 after mirroring: composition at recurring lags with every contact persistent at every length and ring size, at every lag never.

results.title: A cut separates a path across time; a cycle of rings needs one cut per route
results.statement: On rings with rule 60 or 102 and contacts two apart, freezing any one contact of a proved path leaves its far contact needing the first ring at no lag while the other contacts persist, a native separation across time. In four rings closed into a cycle with two routes, one cut removes exactly its route's binomial lag set and a cut on each route separates.

results.title: When a contact shared by two processes binds them at the first step
results.statement: Two rings sharing one contact cell are bound by it at lag 1 exactly when its combiner is XOR or XNOR and neither ring rule is canalizing at its centre, and a self-blind contact binds at lag 1 exactly when its 4 x 4 table has no constant row or column (22,874 of 65,536 laws). With linear or affine rings and an affine contact law the contact binds at lag T exactly when its row of M^T meets both rings.

results.title: Knots across time are minimal decisive sets; pairwise memory is exactly the single ANDs and ORs
results.statement: Written as its space-time law, a deterministic process is a static law on its trajectories, and its knots joining a cell's value after T steps to the first row are exactly that value with the minimally decisive sets of two or more past cells: the sets that, set suitably, fix the future value while no smaller set does. A single deciding cell gives a tie. A nonconstant future value has no knot across time exactly when it is a single conjunction or disjunction of literals, so a process remembers its past only pairwise exactly then. A linear rule with polynomial p has one two-time knot per lag, the support of p^T plus the cell, with |supp p| + 1 places at every lag 2^k; through intermediate rows Ledrappier's law gives 2 + w(T) inside the light cone for T <= 6, and the least knot leaves the light cone at T = 7. In one step of Life the knots are the 70 sets of four neighbours, and the cell's own present is in none.
results.issue: Qualification pending: the third sentence holds for knots joining a future value to the first row. Through intermediate rows a process whose every future value is an AND can still knot two times: rule 128 never shows 1 0 1 after a step, so x(1, 1) and x(2, 4) on force x(1, 2) on, and rules 136 and 160 do the same (see the correction in the TIME-KNOTS-20261107-001 decision note).

results.title: The cut-open torus's spectrum is four copies of a cone's, and at powers of two one return map's
results.statement: The cut-open torus's spectrum is four copies of its quarter-turn cone's, and at powers of two the cone's is one return map of the cut line, whose Smith form is the cone's Jordan data. Computed to side 64 (and the collapse at 128), every eigenvalue is a (2n - 1)-th root of unity of multiplicity k(k + 1)/2 with Jordan blocks 2k - 1, 2k - 5, ...; why at every power of two stays open.

results.title: Doubling every lag keeps every stage balanced by isolating the rings; slower doubling does not
results.statement: A network that splits every ring in four at every lag keeps every stage balanced, because each ring hears only itself and its own cells evolve invertibly, so its contacts' knots are the static stage's. Doubling more slowly lets rings hear each other and loses balance within a few doublings, so here knots across growth and rings hearing each other exclude each other.
results.issue: Qualification pending: the exclusion of knots across growth and rings hearing each other was read at g = 2 only; at g = 3 doubling every 2 or 4 lags keeps every stage balanced while rings hear each other, to 24 x 24 (see ISOLATION-NEED-20261109-001).

results.title: At powers of two the cut-open torus's whole spectrum lives on its two cut lines
results.statement: The cut-open torus's walk is the uncut torus's walk with two lines of contacts deleted; at powers of two the uncut walk dies, so the cut walk's whole spectrum is one 2n x 2n determinant on the cut lines, and every eigenvalue is a (2n - 1)-th root of unity there and at no other side to 64. Whether full reach fails exactly at the powers of two from 8 stays open.

results.title: While the network doubles every lag, no ring hears another; slower doubling makes a horizon
results.statement: When every ring of a running network splits in four at every lag, every contact is reborn before anything reads it, so no ring ever hears another and the grown plane reads no distance while it grows. Doubling every few lags lets each ring be heard only within a fixed radius of the original lattice, a horizon that widens as doubling slows.

results.title: A law grows a network that reads its own distance plainly at every stage, but only a line
results.statement: Inserting one ring at a time into the twist torus of rings, a local rewiring of the three contacts spanning the gap, grows a network whose every stage keeps every contact persistent and reads its distance across time without freezing. Through tori of the regular lattices no growth can do this in two dimensions: an on-time torus of large index is a tube, with balls growing linearly.

results.title: A band inserted while the network runs keeps only the knots it has not reached
results.statement: When the band law adds a band while the network runs, every ring whose influence has not reached the cut keeps all its knots across time and the new band is always bound, but most knots of the rings it has reached lapse. So persistent growth must come between runs, and under continual growth only the newest band stays bound.

results.title: The grown torus reads distance by freezing at every stage, and without freezing only as a ladder
results.statement: Every stage of the band law's torus reads the cut and time lengths exactly, but without freezing only its first stage, the two-ring-wide ladder, reads them, at every size, while every later stage but one small torus needs freezing. Its balls grow like the plane's out to half its loop and then linearly, so band growth makes a tube.

results.title: Honeycomb tori of rings reach every ring only when 3 divides the side
results.statement: On the honeycomb torus of equally spaced rings, influence spreads by powers of the six-neighbour sum over GF(2), and when 3 does not divide the side the ring fixed by the turn of 120 degrees about a ring never needs it, because walks into it cancel across the mirrors. When 3 divides the side every ring needs every ring on every side computed, to 300.

results.title: Composition reaches everywhere at odd index except at digons and the honeycomb's pinned ring
results.statement: On tori of every shape of the three regular lattices, a digon face kills a factor of the walk polynomial so composition cannot reach everywhere (proved), and at odd index that and the honeycomb's turn-pinned ring are the only obstructions apart from one torus of index 63 (computed to index 151). At even index no rule by the lattice mod 16, the torus group's 2-part or its mirrors decides it.
results.issue: Wording qualification: no face of these tori has two sides; read "digon face" as a doubled pair, two contacts consecutive in the same order on both rings they share, which is what the theorem defines (see REROUTE-20261109-001A).

results.title: At powers of two the cut-open torus's eigenvalue multiplicities are Kloosterman sums
results.statement: At sides 2^m every eigenvalue λ of the cut-open torus walk appears K(1/λ)(K(1/λ) − 2)/8 times, K the Kloosterman sum of GF(2n), that is (t² − 1)/8 for the elliptic curve with j-invariant λ, computed exactly for every class to side 128 and every eigenvector count to side 512. These multiplicities provably add up to the whole spectrum, so lower bounds alone would prove that every eigenvalue lies in GF(2n), which stays open.

results.title: No row after the first is open, so knots across time cannot be read from the last growth event
results.statement: Every cell of these networks is read by exactly two cells, so every row after the first has a fixed parity and is not open. Reading knots from the last growth event therefore treats a determined row as open, and read natively from any later row the knots fail even without growth, so the loss under growth while running is real.

results.title: Re-routing keeps every contact persistent, but only lines read their distance plainly
results.statement: Exchanging, at any set of contacts, which ring each arriving ring continues on keeps the contact graph and, at law-(12,12) contacts, the automaton itself, so every re-routing of a lattice torus keeps every contact persistent, and random ones have no flips. Grouped into lines the tori's automata read their distance plainly at every size; on the square contact graph no grouping into small rings does.

results.title: Persistence without a flip comes from pairings of walks to six contacts
results.statement: A contact persists exactly when deleting it keeps det(I + tN) over GF(2), N the contact graph mod 2. Doubled pairs and automorphisms of the contact graph pair closed walks; FLIP-RULE-20261109-001's six-contact example persists by two doubled pairs, and to six contacts every case is paired or flipped, while from seven most are neither.

results.title: Short loops rescue late rings: every torus that reads distance plainly
results.statement: A torus of rings reads distance without freezing exactly when it holds a short loop along which the fastest way to every ring is a single route, the square lattice's (2, 0) and (2, 1) up to the quarter turn and the triangular lattice's vectors of length root 3, or is one of finitely many small tori. The mirror image (1, 2) is late, since rule 60 reads one way round every ring.

results.title: At powers of two the cut-open torus's spectrum is a trace polynomial with matrix coefficients
results.statement: At sides 2^m the cut-open torus's cone polynomial is the determinant of a linearized polynomial in which the trace of GF(2n) has its scalar coefficients replaced by matrices over GF(2), built digit by digit from a one-by-one matrix; without one reversal the same return map has exactly the trace-1 elements of GF(n) as eigenvalues. Why every root lies in GF(2n) is reduced to that determinant and stays open.

results.title: No two shortest routes tie before lcm(m, f) - lcm/m - lcm/f + 1
results.statement: In the contact graph of rule-60 rings on every regular tiling, with m contacts per ring and f per face, no contact is reached by two shortest routes before distance lcm(m, f) - lcm/m - lcm/f + 1, so the plain first need reads every contact closer than that on time. When m = f a tie comes exactly there; elsewhere it does on every tiling read.

results.title: Each eigenvalue's Jordan structure on the cut-open torus is the leading part of one moment matrix
results.statement: At sides 2^m each eigenvalue's Jordan blocks on the cut-open torus are the partial multiplicities of one explicit moment matrix, whose reduction to the eigenvectors has the leading part u⁻¹Y^k L(u²/Y) at every eigenvalue to side 256 (computed). Its leading matrix is invertible for every k (proved), so this is the whole chain lemma 2k − 1 − 4j; its bottom three orders are proved.

results.title: A growing plane reads its original rings' taxicab distance in conformal time, up to a constant
results.statement: For every doubling schedule and every size, counting a lag after k doublings as 2^-k, the first arrival from one original ring to another is 4g times their taxicab distance up to an additive constant, so the round trip is a metric up to 42g + 4. In plain lags the excess grows without bound.

results.title: A grown plane that stops reads the fixed torus's distances
results.statement: A network that splits every ring in four at every lag for k lags and then stops reads, for every ring and every reading, freezes included, exactly what the fixed torus of the grown size reads, with its original rings 2^k ring steps apart per original step. Schedules whose rings heard each other before the stop do not (computed).

results.title: Persistence needs forgetting: no finite substrate has an invertible step and a persistent contact
results.statement: On a finite network an invertible step returns every state to itself, and at that lag each contact holds only its own first value, bound to neither ring, so no contact persists. Hence wherever a contact persists no row after the first is open, for every rule and law, and growth while running cannot be rescued by an invertible substrate.

results.title: Each eigenvalue's Jordan blocks on the cut-open torus follow one polynomial's degree
results.statement: At sides 2^m the eigenvector G·Y^j heads a Jordan chain of exactly 2k − 1 − 4j, k = n/2 − deg G, at every eigenvalue to side 64 and nine of side 128 (computed), so an eigenvalue's multiplicity is read off its one polynomial's degree. Its first order is proved: the reduction is a Hankel matrix of G's norm, giving exactly k mod 2 blocks of size 1.

results.title: Each eigenvalue's eigenvectors on the cut-open torus are one polynomial
results.statement: At sides 2^m the eigenvectors of the cut-open torus at each eigenvalue are one polynomial G times polynomials in Y = k² + k, proved from a self-adjointness and a shared shift ratio, so their number is set by deg G alone. deg G matches the Kloosterman count at every eigenvalue to side 512 (computed); bounding it, and the Jordan chains the collapse needs, stay open.

results.title: Which contact laws make rings native
results.statement: Of the 256 self-blind contact laws, exactly the 32 affine ones that read both arriving cells alike are blind to how rings are routed through a contact, so the 224 others make rings native; an affine law sees the routing only by cutting a ring, so a law under which both rings pass and are seen is nonlinear.

results.title: Tseitin formulas need size 2^Omega(treewidth) on planar and minor-free graphs
results.statement: If every edge outside a bounded set lies on a short cycle with short detours avoiding it, Tseitin formulas need size 2^Omega(treewidth) in resolution and in polynomial calculus with or without twin variables over characteristic other than 2. This covers plane graphs with short faces and d-dimensional grids, and through wall topological minors every graph excluding a fixed minor, planar graphs included (resolution and PCR).

results.title: The depth of a charge hole is cutwidth plus one
results.statement: On a connected graph of maximum degree at most 3, the toggle width equals cutwidth + 1, so an impossible charge network of three-distinction knots is refuted by linear local reasoning over a field that cannot compute in its group exactly at cutwidth + 1. In general the toggle width lies between cutwidth + 1 and cutwidth + floor(maxdegree/2).

results.title: Local holes do not measure how deep a network's hole is
results.statement: In the complex of partial solutions, every knot that excludes two or more states is a hole at its own scope, so the plain hole criterion certifies only the trivial level 2 on parity, sum-mod-3 and not-all-equal networks. How far local reasoning must look is set by the whole network's cuts, not by the shape of its knots.

results.title: The depth of a charge hole is the toggle width
results.statement: Over a field that cannot compute in the charge group, linear local reasoning refutes an impossible charge network exactly once it holds as many distinctions as the graph's toggle width, whatever the charges, while matched rings need one knot. On cubic graphs with up to 10 vertices this depth is cutwidth + 1, and it is not a function of treewidth.

results.title: Tseitin size on all graphs reduces to cellular-or-compact minors, and block-scrambled wall networks defeat the compact case
results.statement: Resolution and PCR size of Tseitin formulas transfers along weak immersions and topological minors, giving 2^Omega(tw^(1/9)/polylog) on every graph and reducing 2^Omega(tw/polylog) to finding a cellular or compact topological minor of nearly full treewidth in every subcubic graph, where immersions add nothing. On walls joined by block-scrambled bundles along an expander, no compact minor keeps the treewidth and cells exist only at scale sqrt(b), a candidate counterexample.

results.title: Polynomial calculus degree of Tseitin formulas is half the carving width
results.statement: Over any field of characteristic other than 2, the polynomial calculus degree of the Tseitin system of a connected graph with an odd charge, written as balanced plus-minus-one binomials and measured modulo y^2 = 1, lies between ceil(cvw/2) and floor(cvw/2) + 1 for carving width cvw, exactly ceil(cvw/2) when cvw is odd. The standard encodings need the larger of the maximum degree and that value, plus at most one before reduction.

results.title: Polynomial calculus size of Tseitin formulas on grids is exponential in the side
results.statement: Over any field of characteristic other than 2, every polynomial calculus refutation (0/1 basis, with or without twin variables) of the Tseitin formula of the a x b grid has size 2^Omega(min(a,b)), and size 2^O(min(a,b)) poly(ab) suffices. Since PCR simulates resolution, resolution needs 2^Omega(min(a,b)) on grids as well.

results.title: Sum-of-squares and Sherali-Adams need size 2^Theta(tw) for Tseitin on graphs built from short cycles
results.statement: A tangle of order k gives Tseitin formulas a pseudo-expectation up to degree k-1 that defeats Sherali-Adams and sum-of-squares, so SoS degree is the carving width up to 4 and Sherali-Adams degree lies between cvw and 3cvw/2. With cell restrictions, SoS and Sherali-Adams size is 2^Theta(tw) on grids, d-dimensional grids, plane graphs with short faces and walls, the first such bounds beyond expanders that we found.

results.title: Hole-faithful refutations of Tseitin formulas need 2^Omega(treewidth); Urquhart's conjecture is the open problem
results.statement: Refutations of Tseitin formulas that never forget a variable at the region where the hole must lie need size 2^Omega(treewidth), because the hole of a random critical assignment stays uniform there and regions fragment size-biased; Davis-Putnam refutations are of this kind. A smaller refutation must re-read variables and forget at the hole's region, and Urquhart's conjecture is equivalent to the open 2^Omega(tw) problem at bounded degree.

results.title: The violated line can be pinned: frozen states block the Tseitin-style width proof
results.statement: In the octahedral knot spaces the violated line is a vortex of a height function, and frozen states pin it: no change within distance 3 moves it to a given adjacent line, in the bulk and in whole-sphere states of K_8, though random states always move. So the Tseitin-style resolution width proof cannot be applied state by state, and width Omega(sqrt n) reduces to a pursuit lemma for flat label states.

results.title: The knot closure is width-3 resolution, and creation is width 4
results.statement: At a gluing line, the crossing knots the elimination closure reaches are exactly the width-3 resolution consequences of the one-sided implicates on at most three variables, derived in depth one or two by resolving only on the line's variables. Every new crossing knot is implied by the same implicates and needs width exactly four, so native creation is the step from width three to width four at a three-variable cut.

results.title: Three-fold spaces are an Euler count: easy for Sherali-Adams, only treewidth-bounded for resolution
results.statement: Refutations of three-fold spaces compose over the handle tree at constant cost per Fano piece, and on a plane core the contradiction is Euler's count of two more faces than lines, which Sherali-Adams of level three refutes. Resolution gets only the treewidth bound 2^O(sqrt n), and solver costs on the octahedral family grow exponentially in sqrt n, so the two-round rule does not compose into a global resolution bound.

results.title: Flat states exist on the whole knot sphere: each corner twists labels by -1
results.statement: Sublattice-and-sign frames on the octahedral knot sphere are flat except at the six corners, each of which twists labels by exactly -1. So for every point z and every six disjoint cuts from z to the corners, one constant label developed over the cut sphere violates exactly one line, through z, and the vortex moves by local re-routing.

results.title: The knot sphere contains Sperner's lemma
results.statement: One-sided 2D Sperner reduces to finding a violated line of the knot sphere by depth-2 decision trees, the violated lines falling exactly in the boundary-oriented full triangles, with the six corners as Sperner's boundary. So query and resolution-width bounds for grid Sperner transfer, and the sphere's width question becomes Sperner's, reduced to an open winding-control lemma.

results.title: The sphere's count needs resolution size 2^Theta(sqrt n)
results.statement: Every resolution refutation of the octahedral knot sphere needs size 2^Theta(sqrt n). Random islands fixed to constant labels kill wide clauses, yet the restricted formula still needs width Omega(sqrt n) because islands add no slack to obstructions.

results.title: The sphere's count needs resolution width Theta(sqrt n)
results.statement: Every resolution refutation of the octahedral knot sphere needs width Theta(sqrt n). Duplicator keeps the vortex where pebbles are sparse, since any obstruction is a closed walk with a bounded number of steps per pebble, so pebbles trap only an area quadratic in their number.

results.title: Grid Sperner needs resolution width Theta(m)
results.statement: Grid Sperner with a fixed boundary needs resolution width Theta(m), and so does Itsykson et al.'s Sperner CSP, for which only tree-like size was known. Walks through the free boundary stay near it, so a full triangle kept deep inside meets only short pebble walks.
results.issue: Qualification pending: "for which only tree-like size was known" is wrong. Dantchev (On the complexity of the Sperner lemma, CiE 2006, LNCS 3988, 115-124) reduces the pigeonhole principle to Sperner's lemma and shows that it has no short constant-depth Frege proofs, which already gives superpolynomial general-resolution lower bounds for Sperner formulas. New, as far as found, are the tight width Theta(m) and, in COUNT-NOTE-20261107-001, the tight size 2^Theta(m).

results.title: Knots compose like cycles exactly in difference laws whose distinctions do not split
results.statement: A law with a Mal'tsev polymorphism composes its knots like cycles, so that any two sharing a distinction leave a constraint once it is forgotten and form matroid circuits, exactly when every subalgebra of its polymorphism algebra has a unique maximal congruence; Boolean laws do exactly when affine. Elsewhere knots fuse or meet at hubs, so cycle-space structure among knots marks difference laws whose distinctions do not split.

results.title: A law recognizes its space rather than creating it
results.statement: A law's allowed states carry a graph exactly when its knot matroid is graphic, and a sphere when it is also cographic: they determine a 3-connected graph exactly and a 2-connected one up to Whitney twists. Presence is decided by Tutte's excluded minors, not by how the law was written, so a randomly written local law can carry a sphere while almost every balanced code carries none; the mathematics is classical.

results.title: Composing knots like cycles reduces to rectangular knots, not to a difference operation
results.statement: Composing knots like cycles does not force a difference operation: parity beside an unrelated law does it without one. The converse reduces exactly to rectangularity of knots, since rectangular knots compose like cycles precisely when no two meeting at a variable split its range; this is proved on two values, and every tested three-variable knot on up to four values supports it.

results.title: Composing like cycles is affine structure modulo the tops
results.statement: A law composes like cycles exactly when its ranges have tops, its ties are bijections modulo them, and a ternary polymorphism is Mal'tsev modulo the tops of its knot ranges, which proves the series' Conjecture 7 through rectangular top images. The tops of knot ranges are then elementary abelian p-groups with polymorphisms acting affinely, and every system carries a direct sum of matroids representable over finite fields, all of which occur.

results.title: Composing like cycles is decided on the tops
results.statement: In every law whose circuits compose like cycles, each system has exactly the circuits of its image modulo the tops, because each variable and its blurred copy are parallel elements; ties become bijections between tops, and every reflexive pp-definable relation lies below its range's top. The earlier conjecture that such laws are Mal'tsev on all their tops fails for disjoint unions, and holds in every sampled law when restricted to the ranges of knot variables.

results.title: Tops can hide any constraint problem
results.statement: Every finite structure is homomorphically equivalent to a law that composes like cycles, and every finite core to a core that does, so composing like cycles alone admits NP-complete constraint problems, even among cores; the core of such a law need not compose like cycles, and it can be non-Taylor. With constants, or for a core with no nontrivial automorphism, composing like cycles does give polynomial time, and both hypotheses are needed.

results.title: Composing like cycles tests codes for linearity and certifies tractability with constants
results.statement: No statement of the composition characterization turned up in a bounded literature scan; its uses are a composition test for linearity of codes, under which the non-Pappus almost affine code fails through an explicit three-copy system, and a tractability certificate for laws that keep composing like cycles with constants. Counting is not covered, and constants can destroy composing like cycles, so whether every such law is tractable is open.

results.title: Composing knots like cycles does not force rectangular knots
results.statement: The local converse and the diagonal lemma are false: a 3-variable knot on four values (x+y+z=0 mod 3 with 3 read as 2, minus (2,2,2)) is non-rectangular, yet its law composes every circuit like cycles because every system keeps the constrained sets of the Z3 law. Composition sees only which sets are constrained, so a dominating difference law hides any fibre pattern inside the components of a fibre graph.

results.title: Latin circuits compose like cycles; Q8 separates Latin from Mal'tsev
results.statement: A law whose circuits are all functional modulo common proper pp-definable equivalences composes like cycles, and among 3-nets of finite abelian groups exactly the p-groups do; every overlapping and non-group candidate tested failed. The 3-net of the quaternion group Q8 survived with Latin knot images yet has no polymorphism Mal'tsev modulo its top, so either it fails in larger systems or Mal'tsev structure on the tops is not forced.

results.title: Loop memory needs block-group-like contact; composing like cycles makes holes twisted finite-field cohomology
results.statement: A knot link remembers a loop exactly when its transfers permute blocks, for any number of values, and in a law composing like cycles its networks remember twisted first cohomology over a finite field modulo the tops, with frame-matroid free sets. The owner's claim holds for two values and fails beyond, through the Z6 and S3 3-nets, dressed parity, and x + y + z = 0 over F3.

results.title: Composing like cycles is a condition on tops, not a classical Mal'tsev condition
results.statement: Composing like cycles is incomparable with congruence permutability, n-permutability and modularity: a lift of the Z3 law is 3-permutable and modular without a Mal'tsev operation, while a shadow of it composes like cycles with neither, its fibre clone having only conjunctions and constants. What the known examples share is a polymorphism that is Mal'tsev modulo each range's maximal congruence, proved for difference laws, their lifts and suitable shadows, and conjectured for all.

results.title: Difference laws that compose like cycles carry only field-representable matroids
results.statement: Single relations carry any matroid as free sets, the Vamos matroid included, but their laws fail; a top lemma shows that group and field laws composing like cycles carry only direct sums of matroids representable over finite fields, one prime at a time, so the Vamos matroid never appears there or in their shadows, lifts and disjoint unions, and every law composing like cycles has tops even without a difference operation.

results.title: Knots composing like cycles form native contact networks relative to a declared substrate
results.statement: Two knots sharing one distinction in a law composing like cycles pass the contact-network gate under recodings, erasure, the law's own restrictions and pp-definitions, with pinning and homomorphic or product transports as the deciding conditions. In a declared substrate the allowed states fix contact adjacency, routes that compose into single contacts, native separation and an extended bond distance, but not the drawing, and the law fixes no substrate.

results.title: No circuit overlaps; Q8's 3-net fails; 3-nets that compose like cycles are abelian p-groups
results.statement: In a law that composes like cycles no circuit overlaps modulo the tops, so composing like cycles is exactly having Latin circuits (multiary quasigroups) modulo proper pp-definable equivalences, while Mal'tsev structure on the tops stays open. The 3-net of the quaternion group Q8 fails through Thomsen's configuration, whose top image is the non-affine relation behind the earlier certificate, and a Latin square's 3-net composes like cycles exactly when the square is isotopic to an abelian p-group.

results.title: Native emergence is approximable except where Fibonacci meets a twist
results.statement: Given McQuillan's winding theorem, native counting with pins is approximable for the 26 windable knots, because the knot axiom K2 is his terraced condition; with the four topological knots this settles 28 of 34. The six left open are the Fibonacci knot with one or two negated places, which escape winding and holography and freeze native trees, as not-all-equal and parity do.

results.title: Emergence is countable exactly when it is topological
results.statement: Gluing topologically is the generalized Fibonacci-gate recurrence, so the four knots that see only the surface count every native network by closed formulas, while the other 30 knots are #P-hard to count given Backens's Holant dichotomy. Closed not-all-equal worlds are an antiferromagnetic Ising model, whose count is a determinant on the sphere.

results.title: Native contradictions are parity contradictions
results.statement: In an unsatisfiable hub-free network of three-place knots, every knot whose removal keeps the network connected allows exactly half of its edge states, so every native contradiction is a set of parity systems joined by forced values, and native networks of every law are decided in polynomial time. Native contradictions are hard for resolution exactly when the law has a parity knot, while hubs carry NP-hardness.

results.title: Any proof that native gadgets cannot clone a bit must be global
results.statement: Rerouting one terminal's arm is injective for each fixed difference pattern, so the arm inequality holds whenever patterns map injectively, as on trees. For gadgets with loops, explicit two- and three-knot gadgets satisfy the inequality but break every local strengthening (per partner, per image pattern, one-sided path flips, the minor form), so any proof must be global.

results.title: Native emergence cannot imitate a hub exactly, and on trees not approximately
results.statement: No native gadget of any knot is an exact hub, and pairs of solutions that do not link all three terminals reroute onto off-diagonal values, which bounds the hub ratio of windable gadgets by the square root of 3 (given McQuillan) and of parity and no-lone gadgets by 1. For the six open knots, tree gadgets are proved to have hub ratio at most 3; gadgets with cycles remain a conjecture.

results.title: Negative curvature forces an antivortex, and finding it is PPADS-complete
results.statement: On the genus-2 double of a holed lattice torus with Kasteleyn signs, the count forces some face to over-agree, and finding such a face is PPADS^dt-complete while finding a violated line or an over-agreeing face is PPAD^dt-complete. A frame developed across the six degree-8 faces carries one antivortex and leaves every line satisfied, and the mirrored Sperner map puts over-agreeing faces exactly in clockwise fully labelled triangles.

results.title: Grid Sperner and the knot sphere need exponential resolution size, with every lemma proved
results.statement: Every resolution refutation of the knot sphere needs width Theta(sqrt n) and size 2^Theta(sqrt n), now with every lemma proved through single-step vortex moves, straight cuts giving d >= (dist - 19)/2, and a row count. Grid Sperner with its fixed boundary, and the Itsykson-Malova-Oparin-Sokolov Sperner CSP, need width Omega(m) and size 2^Omega(m), because with three straight cuts the fixed boundary is a flat state.

results.title: The sphere's count is in PPADS: a degree-3 Sherali-Adams refutation with coefficients +-1
results.statement: The lines' clause falsifiers minus the faces' monochromatic conjunctions sum to exactly 1, a degree-3 Sherali-Adams refutation with 4n - 8 terms and coefficients +-1, so by the unary Sherali-Adams characterization of PPADS^dt (Goos, Hollender, Jain, Maystre, Pires, Robere, Tao) finding a violated line is in PPADS^dt, between one-sided 2D Sperner and PPADS. Cutting-planes and XOR-reasoning solvers do no better than CDCL on it, and whether short cutting-planes or Res(xor) proofs exist is open.

results.title: The knot's count reads the Euler characteristic and is blind to orientation
results.statement: On every closed surface, violated lines minus the faces' excess agreements equals (chi - |D|)/2, where D, the faces the signs make even, has the parity of chi, so the count forces a violated line only on the sphere with Kasteleyn signs and forces an over-agreeing face when chi < |D|. Orientation never enters, and wherever the count forces, the search lies in PPADS^dt, so unlike Sperner it never becomes PPA-hard on non-orientable surfaces.

results.title: Which lattice tori make the knot unsatisfiable
results.statement: On the lattice torus Z^2/L a sign class is satisfiable exactly when the slope triangle conv{(0,0),(p,q),(0,-r)} holds an integer point of matching parity. Hence only degenerate tori, thin tori of circumference sqrt 3 and even index (cyclic chains, solvable in O(log n) queries) and the two Fano tori have an unsatisfiable class.

results.title: The knot sphere's count is PPADS-complete, and its orientation is what keeps it out of PPAD
results.statement: Finding a violated line of the octahedral knot sphere is PPADS^dt-complete and lies outside PPAD^dt, PPA^dt and PLS^dt, so its not-all-equal formula has no polylogarithmic-degree Nullstellensatz refutation over F2 or in unary form although unary Sherali-Adams refutes it at degree 3. Counting monochromatic faces as solutions too, the count becomes PPAD^dt-complete, so the knot's orientation alone separates the two classes.

results.title: Hardness needs a flat disc, not roundness
results.statement: On every two-kind knot sphere the flat states and the Sperner reduction need only a corner-free disc whose rim reaches the six corners, so the knot's contradiction needs resolution width at least a constant times that disc's radius and at most O(sqrt n). Hardness therefore follows the largest flat disc, not roundness: spheres with a flat disc of radius order sqrt(n) are hard without any witness.

results.title: The sphere's count needs exponential size in bounded-depth Frege
results.statement: Every depth-d Frege refutation of the octahedral knot sphere's NAE formula has size exp(n^{eps_d}): the binary left-pigeon principle reduces to SINK, SINK to one-sided grid Sperner and grid Sperner to the sphere by shallow decision trees, and the bijective pigeonhole principle needs exponential size at every fixed depth. Res(xor) and cutting planes remain open.

results.title: Row-linear separation for bit LeftPigeon is a static kernel question
results.statement: For the binary left-pigeon principle, a row-linear polynomial derived in polynomial-calculus degree B, with 2lB - 1 <= n, lies in a fixed kernel of the decoder to Braun's unary pigeonhole system; that kernel contains the inverse-counting identities, summing over holes equals summing over pigeons, and at degree 2 it is a fraction near (l+1)^2 k / v of the row-linear space.

results.title: The extra pigeon closes the decoder route for bit LeftPigeon
results.statement: For the binary left-pigeon principle with n + 1 pigeons coded in l + 1 bits, only one pigeon has the top code bit, so the decoder into the unary pigeonhole principle sends products of top hole bits to zero, and Braun's Res(xor) criterion applied through that decoder certifies only a constant number of lines; the principle with 2n pigeons has no such bit and contains the n + 1 pigeon clauses.

results.title: The sphere's count needs polynomial-calculus degree n^{Omega(1)} over every field
results.statement: Over every field, every polynomial-calculus refutation of the octahedral knot sphere's count has degree at least c n^{1/4}/log n, because a low-degree refutation would give one for the functional pigeonhole principle on an expander. Over F2, tree-like Res(xor) refutations of the count therefore need size 2^{Omega(n^{1/4}/log n)}.

results.title: Degree-based Res(xor) lower bounds cannot reach the sphere's count
results.statement: Braun's generic criterion for Res(xor) size certifies at most exp(d^2/(6v)) nodes for a system refuted in polynomial-calculus degree d, so on the octahedral knot sphere's count, refuted in degree O(sqrt n), it certifies only a constant; carrying Braun's bit-PHP bound to the count would need a parity reduction from PIGEON, which ordinary decision trees cannot give.

results.title: A dag-like Res(xor) bound for bit LeftPigeon reduces to hole-row separation
results.statement: Braun's generic Res(xor) criterion applies to the binary left-pigeon principle with its own clauses, so a superpolynomial dag-like Res(xor) lower bound for this PPADS-complete principle follows from one statement: its row-linear polynomials over pigeon and hole rows stay separated from the polynomial calculus's consequences at degree about 12 k log n for some k = omega(sqrt(n log n)).

results.title: Parity decision trees on the sphere's count need polynomial depth
results.statement: Every parity decision tree that finds a violated line of the octahedral knot sphere, hence every tree-like Res(xor) refutation of its count, has depth at least c n^{1/8}/log n, because a shallow parity tree is a low-degree F2 refutation and the count needs F2 degree polynomial in n. Its size is at least 2 to its F2 polynomial-calculus degree minus 3.

results.title: The binary left-pigeon principle needs exponential dag-like Res(xor) proofs
results.statement: Every dag-like Res(xor) refutation of the binary left-pigeon principle with n holes, with n + 1 pigeons or with 2n, has exp(Omega(n / log^5 n)) lines; the proof runs Braun's bit-PHP framework through a decoder into the unary pigeonhole principle and separates a space of row-linear polynomials that avoids a few spare holes and pigeons.
results.issue: Qualification pending: audited in AUDIT-LEFT-20261110-001, where every step holds (a proof written, V1, conditional on Braun's unrefereed preprint, assumption A55), but the bound is not new in substance: the 2n-pigeon formula is Pudlák and Thapen's rWPHP, and exp(Ω(n)) for it and for the n + 1 pigeon principle follows from Pang's degree–size relation (arXiv 2610.00837, 30 September 2026) by an affine substitution into graph FPHP. The PPADS-complete problem is Reversible-Pigeon in Göös et al., J. ACM 2024.

results.title: The trisum law: the knot's not-all-equal rule one level up
results.statement: A trisum of three non-colourable cubic pieces along a square has amplitude rho1 rho2 rho3 - alpha1 alpha2 alpha3 - beta1 beta2 beta3, where (alpha, beta) splits a piece's colourings by the square point its far line leans to. The knot's not-all-equal rule reappears one level up on the pieces' leanings, and pieces glued further down act only as weights on these two numbers.

results.title: Counting is polynomial on every three-fold space
results.statement: For every three-fold space the colourings with one line removed are counted in polynomial time without any signing: a product over braces, a planar brace one Berman determinant, any other brace a Robertson-Seymour-Thomas trisum tree evaluated with two weighted determinants per planar leaf. Exact counts reach 1720-vertex instances where variable elimination would need factors on 30 variables.

results.title: A gluing carries the harmony when phases cancel
results.statement: The wave reproduces itself on a gluing exactly when six signed sums over phase assignments with mixed corner phases vanish, which phase locking and mirror cancellation achieve up to five triangles and genuine identities achieve later. The law selects thousands of gluings and no growth exponent, so it does not draw a space by itself.

results.title: Three-fold contacts are knots on phases, and the Fano plane is their space
results.statement: At the knot angle a contact of three triangles with odd base count is a not-all-equal knot on their phases, so a gluing of such contacts is the unsigned problem on its dual, which needs seven triangles, and seven suffice. With distinct corner triangles the seven-triangle such gluings are exactly the Fano gadgets, exact for both the signed and the unsigned knot.

results.title: The knot's amplitude is five per handle times Tutte's number per planar piece
results.statement: On every three-fold space the knot's exactness factor is (-1)^(n-1) times a product over the pieces of the space: 5 for each Fano atom (each handle of its surface), 1 for each doubled square, and for each planar piece of glue Tutte's tree-trinity number, the spanning trees of a map for omnitruncation glue. Across a tight cut the count of colourings factors exactly, through a point lemma.
results.issue: Qualification pending: "on every three-fold space" holds when the glue is planar. A non-planar glue piece contributes its own amplitude, which is not Tutte's number and depends on how the piece is glued: 6 for three cubes glued along a square, 13 or 14 for prisms of sizes 2, 3 and 3 (see THREEFOLD-AMPLITUDE-20261030-001B, and Corollary 5 of THREEFOLD-AMPLITUDE-20261030-001C).

results.title: One amplitude for every non-colourable cubic system
results.statement: For every connected cubic triple system that is not 2-colourable, removing any line leaves the same number of colourings, and the transpose gives that number at every point. Counting an Ising weight at half the knot's angle in two orders makes each line's count the average of its points' and vice versa, so every brace has one amplitude, and trisum amplitudes depend on the gluing.

results.title: The knot's three-fold spaces are Fano atoms in planar glue
results.statement: Every such system other than the Fano plane contains at least two Fano planes with one element removed, attached by three-edge cuts; everything else is planar Pfaffian glue (doubled squares, planar braces, and trisums built from them), and every planar cubic bipartite graph occurs as glue. The approved grammar of splices and odd cycles was incomplete: a 43-point system has the cube as glue.

results.title: The knot's three-fold spaces up to 22 points
results.statement: Below 23 points such systems have exactly 7, 13, 19, 21 or 22 points, with 1, 1, 4, 1 and 1 isomorphism classes, each a small core dressed with Fano planes minus an element; none exists at 8 to 12, 14 to 18 or 20 points. With one twisted incidence the sizes are 14, 15, 18, 20, 21 and 22.

results.title: The knot's three-fold spaces are the triple systems that resist 2-colouring
results.statement: Such a gluing is a space for the knot exactly when its dual triple system resists 2-colouring but stops resisting once the corner line is removed, which is the classical even-cycle problem whose one indecomposable exception is the Fano plane. Up to 13 triangles only the Fano plane and its splice occur, and Fano planes splice together without limit.

results.title: Odd cycles of Fano planes
results.statement: A Fano plane minus a line forces its three free points to one colour, so lines meeting it twice act as not-equal constraints, and a cycle of an odd number of such blocks resists 2-colouring. The knot therefore has three-fold spaces with 21, 27, 35 and more triangles built from both classical obstructions to 2-colouring, the Fano plane and the odd cycle.

results.title: The knot's signs are a Kasteleyn structure on its minimal surfaces
results.statement: On every minimal map of every three-fold space with planar glue each face has length 2 mod 4, so the knot's own signs satisfy Kasteleyn's condition; the condition survives every tight-cut splice because exactly three crossing faces form, each joining one face from each side. Non-planar trisum glue behaves the same on all its minimal maps.

results.title: The knot's spin structures are even on every handle
results.statement: Every spin structure induced by the knot's signs and a perfect matching is even, with Arf invariant 0 independent of the matching, and even on every Fano handle; the matchings induce exactly 3^h of them, and on the Fano torus exactly the three even ones, eight matchings each. Odd spin structures for the same signs appear only on non-minimal maps, from genus 3 on.

results.title: The knot's contradiction is a balance of spin sectors, and its amplitude is not spin-local
results.statement: The knot's colouring counts are Arf-signed averages of spin sectors, so its non-colourability is an exact balance of even and odd sectors (8, 8, 8 against 24 on the Fano torus), and its sign class is the only non-colourable one among the surface's Kasteleyn classes. Opening a contact gives 16, 16, 16 and 28, so five per handle does not come from the even spin structures, and at genus 2 the sectors do not factor over handles.

results.title: Fano atoms are handles
results.statement: A three-fold space whose glue is planar has genus equal to its number of Fano atoms, because a piece that keeps its genus when a vertex is deleted adds exactly its genus across a three-edge splice, while in general such splices can lose handles. Its minimal maps are exactly connected sums of the chiral Heawood map, one per atom; the Fano plane's own map is the seven-vertex torus.

results.title: The knot's junction is a similitude, and unbranched twists count in polynomial time
results.statement: At a trisum square, a side carrying the knot's own signs acts on the other closed side as a similitude of the matchgate identity with multiplier alpha^2 + alpha beta + beta^2, the norm of its split at the knot's angle pi/3. So counting stays polynomial under every sign class unless some square has twisted sides on all three branches.

results.title: The knot's junction crosses wires softly, never sharply
results.statement: With nonnegative counts the junction's not-all-equal square lines can never force a relation between the host's two line-neighbours without pinning them, so no junction is a crossover; its points can carry a wire. Yet twisted truncated-octahedron pieces give soft crossings outside the matchgate class, such as (40000, -1112, 3336, -192), so hardness by interpolation remains open.

results.title: Value-free not-all-equal fails on regular systems only at three places
results.statement: For every k >= 4, signed not-all-equal never fails on k-regular k-uniform systems: a minimal failing system would be square with a sign-nonsingular incidence pattern, but its digraph has in- and out-degree at least 3 and is even by Thomassen's theorem. At three places it fails exactly on the knot's Pfaffian spaces, so Thomassen's degree threshold is the two/three boundary for this law.

results.title: No value-free four-place law has mutual selection
results.statement: The 30 value-free four-place knots form four classes: parity's count is polynomial, not-exactly-two and twelve build equality without constants and are NP-complete on 4-regular systems, and not-all-equal never fails. So, unless NP-complete problems are polynomial, mutual selection among value-free laws is special to three places.

results.title: At the knot's law, the knot's atom is a negation
results.statement: A knot's space minus one incidence, placed on an edge, is an exact negation at the knot's law (lam = 0) and multiplies the paths through the edge by a ratio other than +-1 elsewhere (Fano: -141/6079 at lam = 1/2). At the dimer coupling lam = -3 every plain system counts (-2)^n times its perfect matchings, a determinant exactly on the knot's spaces.

results.title: Counting on the knot's spaces: easy only at the knot's law and the dimer law
results.statement: Counting 2-colourings of the knot's spaces with weight lam per monochromatic line is polynomial exactly at lam in {0, 1, -1, -3, oo} and #P-hard at every other complex lam, by chains of atoms and interpolation from the hard Pfaffian systems, with torsion points on the curve of two atom ratios closing the complex case. Beyond the affine couplings only the knot's law (count 0) and the dimer law (a determinant) are easy.

results.title: Parity's weighted family is hard, also where parity fails
results.statement: Counting parity's coupling (weight lam per line missing its parity) on connected simple cubic systems is polynomial exactly at lam in {0, 1, -1, i, -i, oo} and #P-hard at every other complex lam, since the theta substitution turns it into the knot's coupling at lam + 1/lam - 1. It stays #P-hard on systems where parity fails, because a parity certificate survives grafting into any host, so parity's recognisable failures select nothing.

results.title: Five three-place knots, and pinning makes cubic systems hard
results.statement: The 34 three-place knot relations fall into five classes (parity, Fibonacci, not-all-equal, x or (y != z), clause), and only not-all-equal has no preferred value, so only it cannot pin a value. A law that can pin a value, turn a pinned line into an equality and absorb spare occurrences is as hard on cubic systems as with unbounded occurrences, which makes the Fibonacci law and x or (y != z) NP-complete there.

results.title: The knot is the only three-place law with mutual selection
results.statement: Unless NP-complete problems are polynomial, not-all-equal is the only three-place knot whose failing cubic systems are non-empty and recognisable while its count is hard in general; parity is affine, the clause never fails, and the two pinning knots have coNP-complete failures. On plain systems, unconditionally, not-all-equal is the only knot that can fail.

results.title: A plain crossing inside braces
results.statement: Ladders of plain cube junctions with rungs act by (NW)^k with characteristic polynomial (x^2 - 19x - 1)(x^2 + 7x + 13), whose roots, a unit of Q(sqrt 365) and the Eisenstein primes above 13, satisfy the lattice condition, so interpolation over odd k yields an exact crossing. K3,3 is counted from plain Pfaffian braces of 20 to 104 vertices.

results.title: Counting on plain Pfaffian braces is #P-hard
results.statement: Weaving a hard source into a prism frame, with every crossing a ladder of plain cube junctions, gives plain Pfaffian braces (a bond lemma, a cube junction lemma and Hall's condition), so counting on plain Pfaffian braces is #P-hard. Among them planarity and the knot's atom, the Heawood graph, are the polynomial cases found.

results.title: Plain triple systems with Pfaffian incidence graphs are #P-hard to count
results.statement: An unsigned long edge with k capped pairs, read at t = -1 by interpolation over its length, acts as a negation, and lengthening edges inside planar pieces keeps the Pfaffian certificate. So counting proper 2-colourings of 3-regular 3-uniform hypergraphs whose incidence graphs are Pfaffian is #P-hard, and K3,3 is counted end to end from 100 plain Pfaffian instances.

results.title: Plain pages are always twisted, and the Fano plane is the only twist-free plain brace
results.statement: Euler's formula leaves every planar cubic bipartite graph a square face away from any chosen square, where a Pfaffian signing needs an odd sign, so every plain page is twisted and every square of a plain trisum brace has three twisted branches. Since a brace's 4-cycles are nice, the Heawood graph is the only brace whose plain system is not 2-colourable.

results.title: A soft crossing interpolates to a sharp one inside the knot's graphs
results.statement: Repeated k times with capped plumbing, the junction of two twisted truncated-octahedron pages multiplies its four crossing states by 810000, 7506, -22518 and -432 per step, whose prime exponents at 5, 139 and 3 separate them, so interpolation yields an exact crossover inside Pfaffian graphs. Hence counting colourings of every cubic bipartite signed system reduces in polynomial time to counting on cubic bipartite Pfaffian graphs under signings.

results.title: Counting under branched twists is #P-hard: the boundary is two-sided on the knot's graphs
results.statement: Counting colourings of cubic bipartite Pfaffian graphs under signings is #P-hard, by reduction from NAE-3SAT counting through merge paths, dead caps and the sharpened soft crossing, and the instances are twisted on all three branches at every junction. Since the knot's own class and every unbranched twist count in polynomial time, the knot's sign class and the branching of twists away from it divide easy from hard.

results.title: Every failing four-place law builds equality
results.statement: Of the 20 classes of four-place knots, every class that fails on small 4-regular systems builds a link (directly or by lifting a three-point core that realizes the twelve class) and is NP-complete on 4-regular systems, while parity's count is polynomial and the clause and not-all-equal never fail. So, unless NP-complete problems are polynomial, a mutually selecting four-place knot would have to be one of five weak classes, none of which failed in any search.

results.title: On the knot's spaces, junctions are paid for by atoms
results.statement: For every simple Pfaffian cubic bipartite graph other than the Heawood graph and every Pfaffian signing sigma, its Robertson-Seymour-Thomas junctions J, planar braces p and Heawood braces a satisfy J + p <= a + |sigma| - 2, attained by the trisum of three cubes with three edge atoms. So on hypergraphs not 2-colourable without signs every weighted colouring count takes time poly(n) 2^(a-2), while on Pfaffian systems in general counting is #P-hard with no Heawood brace.

results.title: Three ports are free; junctions cost a factor two
results.statement: For 3-regular 3-uniform hypergraphs with Pfaffian incidence graphs, any signs and any weight per monochromatic edge, three-edge tight cuts cost nothing and each 4-sum junction violating the matchgate identity costs at most a factor two at its piece. For 2-colourings only junctions at or above squares with three twisted branches violate it, so counting takes time poly(n) 2^b, between the polynomial unbranched case and the #P-hard branched one.

results.title: Beyond two values, blurring lets a law compose like cycles and count hard
results.statement: The known cycle-composing laws are coset laws with uniform fibres, so they count easily. Doubling a value keeps a law's failures and circuits but makes its count #P-complete, so blurred parity (three values) and blurred Z3 (four values) compose like cycles, fail recognisably and count hard; every Mal'tsev law on three values composes like cycles.

results.title: Which substrates a law fails on: the knot, parity and Z3, and a rigid bridge at four values
results.statement: The knot fails exactly on Pfaffian substrates, always globally; parity where perfect matchings are even, never globally; Z3 everywhere, globally exactly at Z3-corank 1. Blurred Z3 on corank-1 substrates both selects (global failures, easy after removing a line, hard in general) and composes like cycles, but its selected spaces are rigid, only ties, while the knot's can keep a knot.

results.title: The knot's spaces meet only through hubs
results.statement: Across every nontrivial 3-edge cut of a knot's space the line side is exactly the knot (not-all-equal) and the point side exactly a hub (equality), and two sides that both accept knots can fail together only as complementary parity cosets. So the knot's spaces compose natively only through hubs, and a hub-free failing composition is a parity one.
results.issue: Qualification pending: false at 2-edge cuts, where parts meet as two-place parity, and exact only up to signs at 3-edge cuts (see NATIVE-PATHS-20261101-001).

results.title: Two kinds of interface in the knot's spaces
results.statement: Across every nontrivial 2-edge cut of a knot's space one side accepts exactly equality and the other exactly disequality (complementary two-place parity, no hub), and across every nontrivial 3-edge cut the point side accepts exactly an antipodal pair and the line side its complement (a knot against a hub, up to signs). This corrects KNOT-COMPOSE-20261101-001-D001: the knot's spaces do not compose only through hubs.

results.title: Routes in the knot's spaces are fixed by the space and carry one bit at most
results.statement: Every nontrivial 3-edge cut of a knot's space is a proper splice cut or a shifted 2-edge cut, and in ten spaces proper cuts never cross, so the parts and routes are fixed by the space. A route through atoms carries its length mod 2 and a route through a hub nothing beyond it; cutting both routes separates, and these are routes of a declared substrate, not native paths of contacts.

results.title: Knot meets knot only pairwise in the knot's spaces
results.statement: A knot's space stays non-colourable under a twist pattern exactly when the pattern is a cocycle of its incidence graph (sign-nonsingularity and the uniqueness of Pfaffian signings up to switching). Hence if both sides of a nontrivial cut accept knots on its channels, the cut has exactly two edges: knot meets knot only as two-place parity, and three-place emergence never passes between parts without a hub.

results.title: Selection is rigid over fields and for the known non-abelian cycle-composing laws
results.statement: Over a field every global failure of a knot system has corank 1, so removing any line leaves only ties; blurring keeps this, S3 and D_p have only blurred-parity knots on full ranges, and simple non-affine three-value Mal'tsev laws have none. Over Z_(p^k) a failure is global exactly when its class lies in every cyclic subgroup generated by a line's class, and cyclic solution groups leave only ties.

results.title: Selection spends the top layer
results.statement: Global failures over Z_(p^k) with k at least 2 keep knots: signed Z4 does after every removal on a 6-point 4-regular substrate, and on a 9-point cubic substrate, the minimum at three places. Over any finite chain ring a global failure leaves, after any removal, solutions whose top layer is one line, so a kept knot has at most one full-range variable and hides at most k - 1 digits.

results.title: A law that composes like cycles and keeps emergence inside its selected spaces
results.statement: Blurred signed Z4 on five values composes like cycles, fails globally and recognisably, counts #P-complete and keeps knots inside its selected spaces, below its top layer. At two values a law with knots that composes like cycles is affine and hence rigid, while the knot keeps knots inside its selected spaces.

results.title: Selection and cycle-like composition exclude each other
results.statement: Each of the five weak four-place classes yields a knot with a forcing place, and two copies sharing that place form a hub, so none composes its knots like cycles. A Boolean law with a knot whose knots compose like cycles is affine, so its count is 2^(n-r) or 0 and it has no mutual selection: selection and cycle-like composition exclude each other.

results.title: Counted length is a measure on the knot's spaces
results.statement: Across every nontrivial 2- or 3-edge cut of a knot's space each side has one count on its accepted channel values and the two counts multiply to the amplitude, so counted length (its logarithm) is additive over the decomposition: log 5 per Fano block plus the glue's tree-trinity logarithm, independent of the routes' relations and unchanged by transposition. It is a law-intrinsic measure on substrate routes, not a native extended distance.
results.issue: Interpretation pending: whether counted length is a native magnitude has not been decided; read it as a count, not a distance. Qualification pending: the glue's part is its tree-trinity logarithm only when the glue is planar; a non-planar glue piece adds the logarithm of its own amplitude, which depends on how it is glued (see THREEFOLD-AMPLITUDE-20261030-001B).

results.title: Planar glue creates no new emergence; handles do, by three-point knots through the hub
results.statement: On 24 planar knot spaces beyond the census and the planar census, no removal on the planar side creates a knot across the opened cut (2172 removals). Created knots, found only on non-planar sides with six port patterns, have three points: the removed line's hub, a near point and a far point; the first two pin all three ports and the third separates them.

results.title: On a plane knot space the knot fails by counting faces, and selection is a line-face perfect matching
results.statement: With Kasteleyn signs a solution makes each line skip the corner opposite its odd point and every face hold an odd number of skipped corners, so Euler's n + 2 faces for n lines force failure and, after a removal, the solutions are the perfect matchings of the other lines to the faces off the removed line. Genus g removes 2g faces and adds 2g homology parities.

results.title: Selection's hub composes the knot's emergence as a 2-sum
results.statement: Removing a line from a knot's space ties its three points into a hub, exactly the point side of the 3-edge cuts along which the space is spliced from Fano atoms and planar glue. After any removal off a cut's point side the hub holds one bit, and by the knot's symmetry under complementing every value the knots crossing the cut are exactly the 2-sums of a circuit through the hub on each side.

results.title: An opened hub creates emergence that does not compose
results.statement: After removing a line on the point side, the interface is what the closed piece allows on its closing line: one complementary pair (the hub re-ties and the 2-sum holds), two pairs (one port released) or three (the hub becomes a knot). With two or three pairs composition fails, and in the 13-point Fano splice 72 crossing knots arise from no chain of eliminations.

results.title: On a plane side the hub reaches the ports, so pinned knots always have a route
results.statement: Whenever the hub of the removed line and a near point pin the gluing pattern on a plane side, the hub is tied to a non-odd port or forms a near knot with the two non-odd ports one step from the pinned pattern, giving every pinned-and-separated knot an elimination route for any far side. This holds on all 30 plane spaces tested and fails on every pinning of the Fano plane and census 58.

results.title: Cutting a handle open removes its creation only for some cut positions
results.statement: Uniting the knot's near solutions over the four homology sectors of a torus embedding removes all creation for some embeddings and cut positions and not for others, even within one homology class, while dropping one parity removes about nine tenths of the new knots and local point flips remove none. Homology carries most of a handle's creation, but forgetting it is not canonical in point values.

results.title: The access lemma is a theorem: matching potentials are convex on a plane side
results.statement: On a plane knot space minus a line, line-face matchings carry integer potentials forming an L-natural convex set whose parities are values relative to the hub, and rounded midpoints show that a hub pinning never selects a hub-tied port's state and otherwise points one step from the pinned pattern. So every pinned three-point knot through the hub is generated on a plane near side, whatever the far side.

results.title: Crossing knots separated by one port are 2-sums
results.statement: In two knot spaces glued along a three-edge cut, a crossing knot whose excluded pattern one port separates is the elimination, through that port, of its near part plus the port and its far part plus the port, or is tie-equivalent to a one-sided circuit.
